articles.title: The Hand She Couldn't Raise
articles.dek: A concentration camp survivor came face to face with the guard who broke her sister's heart — and found that forgiveness isn't something you feel first. It's something you put on.
articles.quote: Forgiveness isn't a feeling you wait for. It's a garment you put on before you feel like wearing it.
articles.illustration: Corrie ten Boom forgives her Ravensbrück guard
articles.body:
Munich, 1947. A church basement, folding chairs, the smell of damp coats. Corrie ten Boom had just finished speaking about God's forgiveness to a room full of Germans still picking through the rubble of their own guilt. She was Dutch, a former prisoner of Ravensbrück concentration camp, and she had watched her sister Betsie die there — slowly, from the deliberate cruelty of guards who treated starving women like animals. Now she was telling strangers that God could forgive even that.

Then she saw him.

A stocky man in a brown coat was making his way toward her through the dispersing crowd, and the moment his face came into focus, her stomach dropped. She knew that face. She had seen it under a soldier's cap, in a room with a leather whip, at Ravensbrück. He had been one of the cruelest guards in the women's barracks — the one Betsie herself had gone through so much anguish because of.

He didn't recognize her at first. He stuck out his hand and beamed. "A fine message, Fraulein! To think that, as you say, he has washed my sins away!" He told her he had become a Christian since the war. He knew God had forgiven him for the terrible things he'd done as an SS guard at Ravensbrück. And now, he said, could he hear it from her own mouth? Could she forgive him too?

Corrie stood there with her hand at her side, and she could not lift it.

She had preached forgiveness for two years by then. She believed every word of it. But belief and her arm were, in that instant, two different countries. She would later write that it felt like the longest few seconds of her life — the guard's hand still extended, her own heart a cold, immovable stone. She prayed, silently, something close to panic: Jesus, help me. I can lift my hand. That's all I can do. You supply the feeling.

And she raised it. Woodenly, mechanically, she put her hand into his.

What happened next she described as almost physical — a current that started in her shoulder, ran down her arm, and sprang into their joined hands, and with it came a warmth that flooded her whole being, bringing tears to her eyes. "I forgive you, brother!" she cried, "with all my heart." For the first time since the release, she said, she felt the healing that had eluded her for so long.

What strikes me most about that story isn't the ending. It's the order of events. The feeling came after the hand went up, not before. She didn't wait to feel forgiving. She acted forgiving, and the feeling caught up.

That's exactly the sequence Paul lays out in Colossians, in a passage written to people who had never met a Nazi guard but who knew plenty about grudges, grievances, and people who'd wronged them.

"Therefore, as God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you." (Colossians 3:12-13, NIV)

Notice the verb. Paul doesn't say feel compassion, or work up kindness, or wait for patience to arrive. He says clothe yourselves — the same word you'd use for pulling on a coat. It's an action of the will, done with the hands, before it's ever confirmed by the heart. You put on the garment whether or not it fits your mood that morning.

It's worth asking why Paul frames virtue this way instead of just saying "be compassionate" or "feel forgiving." Maybe because he knew what Corrie ten Boom discovered in that Munich church basement: if you wait for your feelings to authorize your obedience, you may wait forever. Feelings are slow. They lag behind decisions. But they do follow — often surprisingly fast — once the decision is made and the hand goes up.

There's a second detail easy to miss. Paul doesn't tell the Colossians to clothe themselves with forgiveness because they're strong enough, or spiritual enough, or have finally processed their pain. He tells them to do it because of who they already are: "as God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved." The identity comes first, in verse 12, before the instruction. You don't forgive in order to earn love. You forgive out of a love that's already settled on you. Corrie's healing didn't earn her God's forgiveness — she'd already received that, years before, in a different kind of unraveling. The hand she raised in Munich was simply putting into practice what had already been true of her since Ravensbrück, since long before that: she was forgiven first.

Maybe you're carrying a name right now. A brother-in-law who said something at a family gathering you haven't been able to shake off. A former boss who let you go without warning. Someone from years ago whose apology never came and probably never will. You've told yourself you'll forgive them when you feel ready. Corrie ten Boom's story — and Paul's word to the Colossians — suggests a different order. Don't wait for the readiness. Raise the hand. Say the sentence, even mechanically, even through gritted teeth: I forgive you. Let the feeling, if it comes, come after.

You don't have to feel warm about someone today to obey God about them today. You only have to be willing to lift your hand and let him supply the rest. That's not weakness pretending to be strength. It's a woman standing in front of the man who broke her family, discovering that grace can move faster than grief — if you just give it your hand.

articles.title: The Wound They Called Fine
articles.dek: Jerusalem's leaders knew how to say the word "peace." What they wouldn't do was actually look at the wound.
articles.quote: Real peace was never the absence of a hard conversation — it's what happens after one.
articles.body:
In barrios across the Philippines, health workers keep running into the same scene. A child steps on a rusty nail in the rice field. Someone grabs a rag, wraps the foot, and says the words every Filipino has heard a hundred times: "Ayos lang 'yan, tumigil na ang dugo." It's fine, the bleeding stopped. The wound is covered. As far as the family is concerned, the story is over.

But barangay health workers know something the rag can't show. Tetanus doesn't care how a wound looks on the outside. It grows in the deep, airless tissue underneath — exactly the environment a puncture wound creates, and exactly the environment a rag wrapped too soon seals in instead of cleans out. That's why community health training in so many provinces now centers on one unglamorous habit: don't just cover the wound. Wash it first — really wash it, deep and long — before you ever reach for a bandage. A wound bandaged without being cleaned doesn't heal. It hides. And what hides gets worse.

Twenty-six centuries ago, a prophet named Jeremiah said almost exactly this about his own nation, and he said it standing at the city gates where everyone could hear.

By the time Jeremiah preached these words, Jerusalem was a generation from disaster. Babylon was rising in the east. Inside the city, the rot wasn't military — it was moral. Jeremiah lists it plainly: people "greedy for gain," leaders who "practice deceit," a society running on exploitation from top to bottom (Jeremiah 6:13). This should have been a five-alarm emergency. The people whose job it was to name that — the priests and the prophets, the nation's designated wound-carers — were the very ones spreading calm instead of urgency.

"They dress the wound of my people as though it were not serious. 'Peace, peace,' they say, when there is no peace." (Jeremiah 6:14, NIV)

Notice they didn't say it once. "Peace, peace" — repeated, like a chant meant to drown out anything that might contradict it. And notice the diagnosis God gives isn't that these leaders were fooled. Two verses earlier he's already said they were greedy and deceitful on purpose. This wasn't an honest mistake. It was a comfortable one. It's worth asking why people who could clearly see decay chose reassurance instead of repair — and the answer is painfully familiar. Honesty costs something. It costs an awkward silence, a strained dinner table, a friendship that gets colder before, if ever, it gets warmer. "Peace, peace" is free. Real peace almost never is.

This same pattern shows up again just one chapter later, when Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and hears people chanting a different kind of comfort: "This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD!" (Jeremiah 7:4). They weren't lying about the building. The temple really was God's house. But they were using that true fact as a shield against an uncomfortable one — that they were oppressing the vulnerable and worshiping other gods right alongside their Sabbath rituals (Jeremiah 7:6–10). Sound familiar? It's the same move as chapter six, just dressed in religious clothes instead of political ones: take something true and comforting, and use it to avoid something true and painful.

Here's the turn worth sitting with: the tragedy of Jeremiah 6:14 was never that the wound existed. Wounds happen to every nation, every family, every friendship. The tragedy is that the people closest to the wound had the standing and the responsibility to name it honestly — and used their standing instead to make everyone feel better about not dealing with it. Real peace was never the absence of a hard conversation — it's what happens after one.

Filipino culture has a beautiful gift for this kind of surface calm. Pakikisama — the instinct to keep things smooth, to avoid away, to let a small offense pass rather than disturb the group — has held families and barangays together for generations, and much of it is genuinely good. But the same instinct that smooths over a seating arrangement can also smooth over a husband's drinking, a sibling's growing debt, a years-old silence between a mother and a daughter who haven't really talked since a wedding went wrong. Everyone in the room can feel the wound. Everyone also knows the unspoken family rule: don't bring it up, don't ruin the mood, just say we're okay. Ayos na tayo. And the wound, uncleaned, keeps doing what wounds do underneath a bandage.

So here's a question worth carrying into this week, aimed gently at yourself before anyone else: is there a wound in your life — in a marriage, a friendship, a family line, your own heart — that's been wrapped but never washed? Not necessarily something dramatic. Sometimes it's as ordinary as a conversation you've avoided for a year because it went badly the one time you tried. Jeremiah isn't calling you to manufacture conflict or dig up every old hurt for its own sake. He's asking something simpler and harder: before you say "it's fine," check whether it actually is.

The good news buried in this hard passage is that God never scolds Jerusalem for having a wound. Every nation, every person, has one. What he grieves is the pretending — because pretending is the one thing that guarantees the wound never heals. The moment you're willing to actually look, clean it out, and let it hurt honestly for a little while, healing becomes possible again. That's not bad news. That's the doorway to the only peace worth having.

This week, pick one relationship you've bandaged without cleaning. Not to blow it up — just to be honest, gently, with one person, or with God, about what's actually underneath. Wash it first. Then let it heal.

articles.title: When Human Help Runs Out
articles.dek: A psalm that dares to name its own disappointment with God — and asks for help in the very same breath.
articles.quote: The prayer that works isn't the one you pray after your doubts are settled. It's the one you pray right through them.
articles.body:
One morning in Bristol, England, sometime in the 1800s, George Müller sat down at a long table with three hundred children who had no parents and no food. The orphanage cupboards were empty. There was no bread, no milk, and no money to buy either. Müller had built his life around a strange rule: he would never ask a single person for money, and he would never let the orphanage's needs be publicized to potential donors. If the children were going to eat, God alone would have to provide it — not a fundraising letter, not a wealthy patron, not a clever appeal.

So that morning, with the plates still empty in front of three hundred children, Müller bowed his head and thanked God for the food they were about to eat. There was, at that moment, no food in the building. Before he had even finished praying, there was a knock at the door. A baker stood there, explaining that he'd woken at two in the morning unable to sleep, feeling strongly that he should bake bread for the orphanage. Minutes later, a milkman's cart broke down directly outside the gate. Rather than let the milk spoil, he gave the entire load to the children. Breakfast was served.

Müller didn't pray that prayer because he'd already worked out where the food would come from. He prayed it into the empty space where an answer should have been. That's the part of the story most people skip past — and it's the exact hinge of one of the more overlooked psalms in the whole book.

Psalm 108 opens like a victory song. David — or whoever compiled these verses from earlier psalms of his — declares that his heart is steadfast, that he will sing and make music, that he will praise the Lord among the nations. Then, in verses 7 through 9, God himself speaks. He claims Shechem and the Valley of Succoth as his own. He calls Gilead and Manasseh his. Ephraim is his helmet, Judah his scepter. This is the language of a king surveying territory he already owns — confident, almost casual.

But then the tone shifts, and it shifts hard. "Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?" (Psalm 108:10). Edom's stronghold sat carved into red rock cliffs, a natural fortress that had humiliated Israel's armies before. And then comes a line that stops you: "Is it not you, God, you who have rejected us and no longer go out with our armies?" (Psalm 108:11).

Read that again. The psalmist is not merely worried about Edom's cliffs. He is naming, out loud, to God's face, a memory of God's own apparent absence. There had been a battle Israel lost. There had been a season when it felt like heaven had stepped back and let them fend for themselves. That disappointment doesn't get resolved in the next line. It doesn't even get answered. It just sits there, raw, unfiltered — and then, without any transition, without any "but now I understand" or "and yet I trust," the very next words are a request.

"Give us aid against the enemy, for human help is worthless. With God we will gain the victory, and he will trample down our enemies." (Psalm 108:12–13)

Notice what didn't happen between verse 11 and verse 12. The psalmist didn't wait until his questions about God's past silence were answered. He didn't need to feel resolved before he could ask for help again. He simply moved — in the same breath — from "you rejected us" to "give us aid." The complaint and the request sit shoulder to shoulder, unreconciled, because real trust was never about having every question settled first.

This is where Müller's empty table becomes more than a nice story. His refusal to ask for human help wasn't stubbornness — it was a lived-out version of verse 12's confession that "human help is worthless" when it's substituted for God rather than received as a gift from him. Müller wasn't against bakers or milkmen. He simply refused to let a fundraising letter replace the praying. He wanted it unmistakably clear, to himself and to every watching child, where the bread had actually come from. And notice — he prayed before the knock at the door, not after. The gratitude came first. The evidence came second.

Most of us do it backward. We wait to pray with confidence until we've already seen the outcome we're hoping for. We want the doubt cleared up before we bring the request. But Psalm 108 suggests something gentler and more useful: you're allowed to bring God your unresolved disappointment and your urgent need in the very same prayer. You don't need a tidy testimony first. You need honesty and a request — and it turns out those can travel together.

Think about what you're actually carrying today. Maybe it's a health scare with no clear diagnosis yet. Maybe it's a job situation where every human option has already been tried and has come up short. Maybe it's simply the tired sense that you've asked for help before and it didn't come the way you expected, and now you're wary of asking again. Psalm 108 doesn't ask you to talk yourself out of that memory. It only asks you to keep speaking anyway — the way David did, the way Müller did at an empty table with three hundred hungry children watching.

Try praying verse 12 today exactly as it's written, out loud if you can: "Give us aid against the enemy, for human help is worthless." Let it be a plain admission that you've reached the end of what people around you can fix. Then let verse 13 follow it, not as a guarantee of exactly how or exactly when, but as the settled ground underneath the request: with God, this will not end the way it looks like it might end right now. The knock at the door doesn't always come the same morning. But the prayer was never waiting on the knock. It was only ever waiting on you.

articles.title: The Letter Lincoln Never Sent
articles.dek: A wartime grudge, a locked drawer, and an ancient proverb about the offense that's better covered than repeated.
articles.quote: Covering an offense isn't weakness or denial. It's a small, everyday rehearsal of the same mercy God shows us.
articles.body:
In July 1863, Abraham Lincoln sat down to write one of the angriest letters of his presidency — and then he did something almost no one does with anger that hot. He never sent it.

General George Meade had just won the Battle of Gettysburg, but instead of chasing Robert E. Lee's battered army and finishing the war then and there, Meade let it slip back across the swollen Potomac River and escape into Virginia. Lincoln was convinced the war could have ended in that one week. He believed Meade had let victory itself walk out the door. So he picked up his pen and wrote Meade a letter that laid out every failure in plain, cutting language — the missed chance, the wasted lives, the cost of hesitation.

Then he folded it, wrote across the top, "never sent, or signed," and put it in a drawer.

It wasn't the only one. Historians who later went through Lincoln's papers found a small stack of these — letters written in the heat of real grievance, addressed to real people who had genuinely wronged him, and never mailed. He called the practice, half-joking, a way to "let off steam." He'd write out the whole complaint, sharp and specific, and then simply not send it. The anger got its say. It just never got an audience.

Now turn to a strange little verse tucked into a chapter that's mostly one-liners about family, fools, and friendship.

Whoever would foster love covers over an offense, but whoever repeats the matter separates close friends. (Proverbs 17:9, NIV)

It sounds almost too simple to be wisdom. Of course keeping quiet about a wrong preserves a friendship — everyone knows that. But sit with the verse a little longer and it starts to do more work than it first seems.

Notice the two verbs Solomon sets against each other: covers and repeats. Neither one pretends the offense never happened. The Hebrew word behind "covers" is the same word-family used elsewhere in the Old Testament for how sin itself gets dealt with. When David writes, "Blessed is the one whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sin is covered" (Psalm 32:1), it's the same picture: not erased from history, not denied, but covered — dealt with, absorbed, no longer held up for display. Proverbs 17:9 is quietly borrowing the language of atonement and applying it to something as ordinary as a friend who hurt your feelings.

Covering an offense isn't weakness or denial. It's a small, everyday rehearsal of the same mercy God shows us. It costs something — real anger, real grievance, real cause to complain — and chooses to absorb it rather than pass it on.

The other half of the verse is where it gets uncomfortable. "Whoever repeats the matter separates close friends." Not enemies — close friends. The word for "repeats" doesn't necessarily mean lying about what happened. It can simply mean going over it again — telling it to one more person, rehearsing it one more time, keeping the wound fresh by talking about it instead of letting it close. Solomon isn't only warning against slander. He's warning against something far more common and far more respectable: the retelling that feels justified every single time you do it, and that quietly, one conversation at a time, ends a friendship you never meant to lose.

Lincoln understood something about that instinct. He wasn't a passive man, and he wasn't naive about Meade's mistake — the unsent letter proves he felt every bit of the anger. But he seemed to know that the letter, once sent, could never be unsent. Once Meade read it, once it was repeated to a third person, once it became part of the story people told about that summer, it would do damage that couldn't be undone — to Meade, to the army's morale, maybe to the war effort itself. So Lincoln let the anger exist on paper, fully and honestly, and then chose not to let it travel any further. Meade served under Lincoln for the rest of the war, and Lincoln never mentioned the letter again. History remembers Gettysburg as a victory. It rarely remembers the quieter one Lincoln won at his own desk, over his own worst impulse.

This is not a call to swallow every hurt in silence, or to stay in relationships where real harm keeps happening — Proverbs elsewhere has plenty to say about confronting a matter directly and wisely with the person involved: "Better is open rebuke than hidden love" (Proverbs 27:5). Covering an offense in 17:9 isn't the same as hiding from it. It's the discipline of not multiplying it — not by telling five friends, not by bringing it up again every time you're annoyed, not by letting one wound become the lens through which you now see the whole person.

Most of us will never write a letter to a Civil War general. But almost all of us have written the modern version — the group chat message drafted at 11 p.m., the retelling that starts with "you won't believe what she said to me," the comment we're already planning to make the next time the subject comes up. Proverbs 17:9 asks a simple, searching question before any of that: will this foster love, or will it just repeat the matter? Worth asking before we hit send — and worth asking again before we bring it up for the third time this month.

Here is what makes this good news and not just good advice. The proof that covering an offense is worth it isn't only Lincoln's drawer of unsent letters. It's the cross. There, the ultimate offense — every sin, fully known, fully deserving judgment — was covered, absorbed, paid for, so it would never have to be repeated against us. That's the love Proverbs 17:9 is quietly inviting us into: not a love that pretends nothing happened, but a love willing to absorb the cost of an offense so it stops traveling.

So the next time someone wrongs you — small or large — try writing the letter if you need to. Say the whole true, sharp thing on paper, in a text you never send, in a prayer God can handle. Let the anger have its say. Then ask yourself the question Lincoln seemed to already know the answer to: does the world actually need this sent? Or has it already done what it needed to do, right there, in the covering?
